missing_facts: Whether Robyn Ellis paid sufficient Income Tax or Capital Gains Tax in the 2025-26 tax year
Whether Robyn Ellis completed a Gift Aid declaration for the £260 payment
Whether the £260 payment was routed through a Payroll Giving scheme
justification: The evidence overwhelmingly indicates that the £260 received on 4 February 2026 is a payment for advertising services rather than a donation, which disqualifies it from Gift Aid under E10. The booking correspondence shows Robyn Ellis, who runs a grooming salon, asked for a newsletter booking link and six-week homepage feature; the coordinator quoted exactly £260 for those two placements; Robyn confirmed the amount 'worked for her'; the booking sheet was marked 'awaiting settlement' until the £260 arrived, at which point it moved to 'confirmed'; and the placements subsequently appeared in the agreed locations. The only contrary characterisations are the spreadsheet label 'donation', Robyn's message about helping animals, and a volunteer's note admitting 'we didn't raise an invoice, so I called it a donation' — the last of which is an internal accounting label applied after the fact and does not change the commercial substance of the transaction. The substance of the arrangement is a quid pro quo: £260 in exchange for two advertising placements. Under E10, Gift Aid cannot be claimed on payments that are a payment for goods or services. Atom a6 is therefore FALSE on the weight of the evidence, and because all conditions must be satisfied (ALL gate in the eligibility expression), Gift Aid cannot be claimed on this payment. The remaining unresolved conditions (a3, a4, a5, a7) are immaterial because the disqualifying condition a6 is already established. The separate £20 cash gift from the December collection event is outside the scope of this analysis.
scope_issues: The £260 payment and the separate £20 cash gift from Robyn Ellis at the December collection event are two distinct transactions; this analysis covers only the £260 February payment as specified.

The policy passages do not define the monetary threshold for a donor benefit under E11, so even if the £260 were treated as a donation, it could not be determined from the passages alone whether the advertising placements exceed the permitted limit — however this is moot given the a6 finding.

ir_discrepancies.description: The intermediate representation marks a6 as 'CONFLICTING' and a7 as 'CONFLICTING', treating the characterisation of the payment as genuinely ambiguous. However, on a proper weighing of the evidence, the commercial substance of the £260 is clearly a payment for advertising services: the quote matched the payment exactly, the booking sheet moved to confirmed on receipt, and the placements were delivered. The volunteer's after-the-fact label of 'donation' and Robyn's stated charitable sentiment do not override the commercial substance. The correct status for a6 is FALSE (payment for services), making the conflict characterisation misleading and understating the strength of the disqualifying evidence.

The intermediate representation marks a5 (not made through Payroll Giving) as UNKNOWN, citing absence of explicit confirmation. Given that the payment arrived by direct debit from an individual running a small grooming salon in the context of an advertising arrangement, there is no realistic basis to treat Payroll Giving as a live possibility. While technically unconfirmed, treating this as a meaningful unknown overstates the uncertainty; it is practically TRUE. This does not affect the outcome but is a minor overstatement of uncertainty.
